images.alt: The Birth of Venus by Sandro Botticelli, c. 1485. Uffizi Gallery, Florence.
images.caption: The Birth of Venus — Sandro Botticelli, c. 1485. The goddess emerges from the sea on a scallop shell.

images.alt: Venus de Milo, c. 130–100 BCE. Louvre Museum, Paris.
images.caption: Venus de Milo — Alexandros of Antioch, c. 130–100 BCE. The most famous Aphrodite in the world.

images.alt: Capitoline Venus. Capitoline Museums, Rome.
images.caption: Capitoline Venus — Roman copy of a Hellenistic original. The goddess modestly covers herself, establishing the type for Western beauty.

images.alt: Aphrodite of Knidos by Praxiteles, Roman copy. Glyptothek, Munich.
images.caption: Aphrodite of Knidos — Praxiteles, 4th century BCE. The first life-sized nude statue of a goddess in Greek art.

images.alt: Venus Anadyomene by Titian, c. 1520. Scottish National Gallery, Edinburgh.
images.caption: Venus Anadyomene — Titian, c. 1520. The goddess wrings sea foam from her hair.

images.alt: The Judgement of Paris by Peter Paul Rubens, c. 1636. National Gallery, London.
images.caption: The Judgement of Paris — Peter Paul Rubens, c. 1636. The moment Aphrodite won the golden apple and doomed Troy.

images.alt: Venus and Mars by Sandro Botticelli, c. 1485. National Gallery, London.
images.caption: Venus and Mars — Sandro Botticelli, c. 1485. Love defeats war in this dreamlike allegory of desire and conflict.

images.alt: Venus de' Medici. Uffizi Gallery, Florence.
images.caption: Venus de' Medici — Roman copy. Once the most copied statue in Europe, defining feminine beauty for centuries.

images.alt: Aphrodite Anadyomene, marble statue. Louvre Museum.
images.caption: Aphrodite Anadyomene — Marble statue, Louvre. The goddess wrings sea-foam from her hair in the type that celebrated her birth from the waves.

images.alt: Apollo Belvedere, Roman copy. Vatican Museums.
images.caption: Apollo Belvedere — Roman copy of a Greek original by Leochares, c. 330 BCE. The ideal of male beauty and divine composure.

images.alt: Apollo Belvedere full view. Vatican Museums.
images.caption: Apollo Belvedere (full) — The god stands in contrapposto, having just released an arrow from his bow.

images.alt: Apollo Lykeios, Roman copy. Louvre Museum, Paris.
images.caption: Apollo Lykeios — The god rests on a support, a mantle draped over his arm. Found at the Lyceum gymnasium in Athens.

images.alt: Apollo Sauroktonos by Praxiteles, Roman copy. Louvre Museum.
images.caption: Apollo Sauroktonos — Praxiteles, c. 350 BCE. The young god leans against a tree, about to spear a lizard.

images.alt: Ruins of the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, Greece.
images.caption: Temple of Apollo at Delphi — The omphalos, the navel of the world. Where the Pythia spoke prophecy.

images.alt: Apollo and Daphne by Gian Lorenzo Bernini, 1622–1625. Galleria Borghese, Rome.
images.caption: Apollo and Daphne — Gian Lorenzo Bernini, 1622–25. Marble transformed into living flesh, bark, and laurel leaves.

images.alt: Apollo slaying Python, Attic red-figure pelike, c. 460 BCE. Louvre Museum.
images.caption: Apollo Slaying Python — Attic red-figure pelike, c. 460 BCE. The god avenges his mother by killing the serpent.

images.alt: Apollo Citharoedus, Roman statue. Capitoline Museums, Rome.
images.caption: Apollo Citharoedus — The lyre-player. Music so perfect it could charm stones and bend the will of gods.

images.alt: Apollo, Roman copy. Hermitage Museum, Saint Petersburg.
images.caption: Apollo — Roman copy, Hermitage Museum. The archer god, perfect in form, terrible in wrath.

images.alt: Ares Ludovisi, Roman copy. Palazzo Altemps, Rome.
images.caption: Ares Ludovisi — Roman copy of a Greek original. The god of war sits in restless stillness, helmet beside him.

images.alt: Ares Borghese, Roman copy. Louvre Museum, Paris.
images.caption: Ares Borghese — The muscular torso of the war god, stripped of armor, raw violence made flesh.

images.alt: Mars and Venus Surprised by Vulcan by Tintoretto.
images.caption: Ares and Aphrodite — Attic red-figure, c. 360 BCE. The lovers trapped in Hephaestus's net, exposed to the laughter of Olympus.

images.alt: Ares, fresco from the Temple of Ares at Paestum.
images.caption: Ares at Paestum — The war god in South Italian fresco, grim and unsmiling.

images.alt: Ares, Roman statue. Vatican Museums.
images.caption: Ares — Roman statue, Vatican Museums. The face of war: beautiful, blank, and utterly merciless.

images.alt: Athena Parthenos replica by Alan LeQuire. Nashville Parthenon.
images.caption: Athena Parthenos — Alan LeQuire replica, Nashville Parthenon. The colossal gold-and-ivory original by Phidias stood 12 meters tall.

images.alt: Athena of Velletri, Roman copy. Louvre Museum, Paris.
images.caption: Athena of Velletri — Roman copy of a Greek original. The aegis raised, the Gorgoneion at her breast, eyes that see everything.

images.alt: Bust of Athena Velletri type, Glyptothek, Munich.
images.caption: Pallas Athena — Velletri type, Glyptothek, Munich. The spear rests against her shoulder. She does not need to raise it.

images.alt: Athena Giustiniani, Roman copy. Vatican Museums.
images.caption: Athena Giustiniani — Vatican Museums. The aegis draped over her shoulders, the owl at her feet. Wisdom made stone.

images.alt: Attic black-figure Athena Promachos by the Burgon Group, c. 560 BCE.
images.caption: Athena Promachos — Attic black-figure by the Burgon Group, c. 560 BCE. "She who fights in the front line." Public domain via Wikimedia Commons.

images.alt: Athena Lemnia, reconstruction. Dresden.
images.caption: Athena Lemnia — Phidias's lost masterpiece, reconstructed. The most beautiful Athena ever made.

images.alt: Athena and Marsyas, Mykonos vase, c. 440 BCE.
images.caption: Athena and Marsyas — Mykonos vase, c. 440 BCE. The moment before the satyr is flayed for challenging the gods.

images.alt: The Birth of Athena, black-figure amphora c. 550 BCE, Louvre F 32.
images.caption: The Birth of Athena — Black-figure amphora, c. 550 BCE. Louvre, Paris (F 32). She springs fully armed from Zeus's head. Public domain via Wikimedia Commons.

images.alt: Helmeted head of Athena, National Archaeological Museum, Athens, inv. 1763.
images.caption: Helmeted Athena — National Archaeological Museum, Athens (inv. 1763). The face beneath the Corinthian helmet: calm, knowing, and utterly unafraid. Public domain via Wikimedia Commons.

images.alt: Zeus of Otricoli, Roman copy. Vatican Museums.
images.caption: Zeus of Otricoli — Roman copy, Vatican Museums. The king of gods in mature majesty, beard curled, brow thunderous.

images.alt: Artemision Bronze, c. 460 BCE. National Archaeological Museum, Athens.
images.caption: Artemision Bronze — c. 460 BCE. Zeus or Poseidon? The arm is raised to throw — thunderbolt or trident?

images.alt: Zeus and Ganymede, terracotta group from Olympia c. 480-470 BCE, Metropolitan Museum (on loan).
images.caption: Zeus and Ganymede — Terracotta group from Olympia, c. 480–470 BCE. The eagle-god seizes the Trojan prince. The Metropolitan Museum, New York (on loan, L.1999.10.14). Public domain via Wikimedia Commons.

images.alt: Zeus, marble statue. National Archaeological Museum, Athens.
images.caption: Zeus — National Archaeological Museum, Athens. The thunderer at rest, but never relaxed.

images.alt: Jupiter of Smyrna, Roman copy. Louvre Museum.
images.caption: Jupiter of Smyrna — Louvre Museum. The Roman Zeus: same power, different name, equally terrible.

images.alt: Hades, detail from the Judgement of Paris, Attic black-figure amphora, c. 550 BCE.
images.caption: Hades — Attic black-figure, c. 550 BCE. The unseen king, rarely depicted, for mortals feared to speak his name.

images.alt: Hades and Persephone, Attic red-figure krater, c. 430 BCE. British Museum.
images.caption: Hades and Persephone — Attic red-figure, c. 430 BCE. The king and queen of the dead, enthroned in shadows.

images.alt: Serapis as Pluto with Cerberus, Roman sculpture from the Villa of Chiragan. Musée Saint-Raymond, Toulouse.
images.caption: Pluto with Cerberus — Roman sculpture from the Villa of Chiragan, Musée Saint-Raymond, Toulouse. Hades as Serapis-Pluto, guardian of the dead, with his three-headed hound.

images.alt: Heracles and Cerberus, Attic black-figure amphora, c. 525 BCE. British Museum.
images.caption: Cerberus — Attic black-figure, c. 525 BCE. The hound of Hades, three-headed guardian of the threshold.

images.alt: Odysseus in the underworld, Attic red-figure krater, c. 450 BCE. Louvre Museum.
images.caption: The Nekyia — Odysseus summons spirits in Hades. The underworld as the Greeks imagined it.

images.alt: Persephone and Hades, detail. British Museum.
images.caption: The Rape of Persephone — The moment the underworld gained its queen, and the world gained winter.

images.alt: Hecate Chiaramonti, Roman copy. Vatican Museums.
images.caption: Hecate Chiaramonti — Vatican Museums. The triple-bodied goddess, guardian of crossroads and protector of the home.

images.alt: Statue of Hecate, 3rd century AD, Antalya Museum, Turkey.
images.caption: Hecate of Antalya — 3rd century AD. The triple-formed goddess stands with her torches, guardian of necropolis and night.

images.alt: Hecate fighting Klytios on the Pergamon Altar, c. 180 BCE. Pergamon Museum, Berlin.
images.caption: Hecate on the Pergamon Altar — c. 180 BCE. The goddess battles the Giant Klytios alongside Artemis, torches blazing in marble fury.

images.alt: Hecate statue, Antalya Museum.
images.caption: Hecate — Antalya Museum. The goddess of crossroads preserved in a Roman-period statue, eyes fixed on the boundaries between worlds.

images.alt: Triple Hecate statue, Roman period, Afyonkarahisar Archaeological Museum.
images.caption: Triple Hecate — Roman period, 2nd century AD. Three bodies, three faces, watching every direction at the crossroads.

images.alt: Artemis-Hekate, 3rd century BCE, Archaeological Museum of Tirana.
images.caption: Artemis-Hekate — 3rd century BCE, Apollonia. A limestone fusion of huntress and goddess of the crossroads, protector of the necropolis.

images.alt: Artemision Bronze, c. 460 BCE. National Archaeological Museum, Athens.
images.caption: Artemision Bronze — c. 460 BCE. Poseidon or Zeus? The god of the sea in his most famous bronze form.

images.alt: Poseidon statue, sea god with trident.
images.caption: Poseidon — Roman copy, Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek. The earth-shaker, beard tangled like seaweed, eyes like storm waves.

images.alt: Temple of Poseidon at Sounion, Greece.
images.caption: Temple of Poseidon at Sounion — Perched on the cliff edge where the Aegean meets the sky. Sailors saw this first on their return to Athens.

images.alt: Poseidon, Roman copy. British Museum.
images.caption: Poseidon — British Museum. The sea god stands with his trident, master of earthquakes and tides.

images.alt: Poseidon of Melos, Roman copy. Louvre Museum.
images.caption: Poseidon of Melos — Louvre Museum. The calm before the storm, the sea at rest but never tame.

images.alt: Poseidon and Amphitrite, Attic red-figure krater, c. 470 BCE. British Museum.
images.caption: Poseidon and Amphitrite — Attic red-figure, c. 470 BCE. The sea king and his queen in their chariot drawn by sea creatures.

images.alt: Hermes and the Infant Dionysus by Praxiteles, c. 340 BCE. Archaeological Museum of Olympia.
images.caption: Hermes and the Infant Dionysus — Praxiteles, c. 340 BCE. The messenger god carries the divine child, one of the most tender images in Greek art.

images.alt: Hermes Ludovisi, Roman copy. Palazzo Altemps, Rome.
images.caption: Hermes Ludovisi — Roman copy. The god rests, his caduceus beside him, winged sandals unstrapped.

images.alt: Hermes Ingenui, Roman copy. Louvre Museum.
images.caption: Hermes Ingenui — Louvre Museum. The youthful messenger, eternally between worlds.

images.alt: Hermes Psychopompos, Attic red-figure krater, c. 430 BCE. Louvre Museum.
images.caption: Hermes Psychopompos — Attic red-figure, c. 430 BCE. The guide of souls leads the dead to the underworld.

images.alt: Hermes, Roman copy. Villa Paolina, Rome.
images.caption: Hermes — Villa Paolina. The divine herald, protector of travelers, thieves, and merchants.

images.alt: Hermes, Roman copy. Prado Museum, Madrid.
images.caption: Hermes — Prado Museum. The god of boundaries, standing at the threshold between Olympus and Earth.

images.alt: Demeter Chiaramonti, Roman copy. Vatican Museums.
images.caption: Demeter Chiaramonti — Vatican Museums. The grain goddess, mother of Persephone, giver of seasons.

images.alt: Demeter, Roman copy. Getty Villa, Malibu.
images.caption: Demeter — Getty Villa. The mother who searches the earth for her lost daughter.

images.alt: Demeter and Persephone, Attic red-figure krater, c. 450 BCE. British Museum.
images.caption: Demeter and Persephone — Attic red-figure, c. 450 BCE. The reunion of mother and daughter: the birth of spring.

images.alt: Demeter of Eleusis, c. 330 BCE. Archaeological Museum of Eleusis.
images.caption: Demeter of Eleusis — c. 330 BCE. The mysteries of grain and rebirth, kept secret for two thousand years.

images.alt: Demeter Cnidia, Roman copy. British Museum.
images.caption: Demeter Cnidia — British Museum. The goddess of the harvest, crowned with wheat.

images.alt: Demeter and Triptolemus, Attic red-figure krater, c. 480 BCE. Louvre Museum.
images.caption: Demeter and Triptolemus — Attic red-figure, c. 480 BCE. The goddess teaches the prince of Eleusis to sow grain.

images.alt: Statue of Persephone at Eleusis, Roman period.
images.caption: Persephone of Eleusis — Roman period. Queen of the underworld, daughter of spring, goddess of both life and death.

images.alt: Persephone of Eleusis, Archaeological Museum of Eleusis.
images.caption: Persephone of Eleusis — The Kore who became Queen, innocence transformed into sovereignty in the mystery sanctuary.

images.alt: Persephone and Hades, Attic red-figure krater, c. 430 BCE. British Museum.
images.caption: Persephone and Hades — Attic red-figure, c. 430 BCE. The queen and king of the dead, enthroned in shadows.

images.alt: The Return of Persephone by Frederic Leighton, 1891.
images.caption: The Return of Persephone — Frederic Leighton, 1891. The reunion with Demeter that brings spring back to the world.

images.alt: Pluto-Serapis and Persephone-Isis, Archaeological Museum of Heraklion.
images.caption: Pluto-Serapis and Persephone-Isis — Archaeological Museum of Heraklion. The Greco-Egyptian fusion of underworld king and queen.

images.alt: Hades abducting Persephone, Apulian red-figure dish by the Underworld Painter.
images.caption: The Rape of Persephone — Apulian red-figure, by the Underworld Painter. The moment Hades seized her, and the world gained winter.

images.alt: Artemis of Versailles, Roman copy. Louvre Museum, Paris.
images.caption: Artemis of Versailles — Louvre Museum. The huntress draws an arrow from her quiver, dogs at her feet.

images.alt: Artemis Brauronia, Roman copy. British Museum.
images.caption: Artemis Brauronia — British Museum. The goddess of the bear, protector of young women.

images.alt: Diana of Versailles, Roman copy. Louvre Museum.
images.caption: Diana of Versailles — The Roman Artemis: huntress, moon goddess, protector of the wild.

images.alt: Artemis and Actaeon, Attic red-figure krater, c. 450 BCE. British Museum.
images.caption: Artemis and Actaeon — Attic red-figure, c. 450 BCE. The hunter who saw too much, transformed into a stag by the virgin goddess.

images.alt: Artemis killing the children of Niobe, Attic red-figure krater, c. 460 BCE. Louvre Museum.
images.caption: Artemis and the Children of Niobe — Attic red-figure, c. 460 BCE. The terrible vengeance of a goddess mocked.

images.alt: Artemis of Ephesus, Roman copy. Ephesus Archaeological Museum.
images.caption: Artemis of Ephesus — The many-breasted goddess of the great temple, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

images.alt: Roman sarcophagus with Dionysus and Ariadne, c. 230–240 CE. Louvre Museum.
images.caption: Dionysus and Ariadne Sarcophagus — c. 230–240 CE. The wine god discovers Ariadne on Naxos; vines and revelers frame their union.

images.alt: Dionysus sailing among pirates, Attic black-figure kylix by Exekias, c. 530 BCE. Staatliche Antikensammlungen, Munich.
images.caption: Dionysus in His Ship — Black-figure kylix by Exekias, c. 530 BCE. Pirates who seized the god are transformed into dolphins as vines overtake the mast.

images.alt: Feast of Dionysus with maenads and silens, Attic red-figure lebes by the Dinos Painter, c. 420 BCE.
images.caption: Feast of Dionysus — Red-figure lebes by the Dinos Painter, c. 420 BCE. Maenads and silens whirl around the god in ecstatic communion.

images.alt: Resting Satyr, companion of Dionysus, Roman copy after Praxiteles.
images.caption: Resting Satyr — Roman copy after Praxiteles. The woodland companion of Dionysus leans on a tree trunk, embodying the god's untamed retinue.

images.alt: Theatre of Dionysus, Athens.
images.caption: Theatre of Dionysus — Athens. Where tragedy and comedy were born from the god's sacred rituals.

images.alt: Bacchus by Caravaggio, c. 1596. Uffizi Gallery, Florence.
images.caption: Bacchus — Caravaggio, c. 1596. The god of wine as a young man, offering the viewer a glass of his own divinity.

images.alt: Prometheus Bound by Peter Paul Rubens, c. 1612. Philadelphia Museum of Art.
images.caption: Prometheus Bound — Peter Paul Rubens, c. 1612. The Titan chained to the Caucasus, liver torn by the eagle of Zeus.

images.alt: Henry Fuseli, Hephaestus, Bia and Crato Securing Prometheus on Mount Caucasus.
images.caption: Prometheus Bound — Henry Fuseli. The Romantic vision: agony as sublime defiance, watched by powers of Olympus and Earth.

images.alt: Prometheus and satyrs with torches, Attic red-figure dinos, c. 420 BCE.
images.caption: Prometheus with Satyrs and Torches — Attic red-figure dinos, c. 420 BCE. The fire-bringer stands amid the ecstatic retinue of Dionysus.

images.alt: Heracles freeing Prometheus, Attic red-figure volute krater, c. 400 BCE. National Archaeological Museum, Athens.
images.caption: Heracles Frees Prometheus — Attic red-figure volute krater, c. 400 BCE. The hero shoots the eagle, ending the Titan's eternal torment.

images.alt: Atlas and Prometheus, Laconian kylix by the Arkesilas Painter, c. 565–560 BCE. Vatican Museums.
images.caption: Atlas and Prometheus — Laconian kylix by the Arkesilas Painter, c. 565–560 BCE. The Titan holds the heavens while the fire-bringer looks on, serpent coiled below.

images.alt: Medusa Rondanini, Roman copy. Glyptothek, Munich.
images.caption: Medusa Rondanini — Glyptothek, Munich. The gorgon's face transformed from horror into pathos: she weeps even in stone.

images.alt: Medusa Rondanini, Roman copy after Phidias. Glyptothek, Munich.
images.caption: Medusa Rondanini — Roman copy after Phidias, Glyptothek. The most famous gorgoneion in Western art.

images.alt: Perseus pursuing Medusa, Attic black-figure band-cup.
images.caption: Perseus Pursuing Medusa — Attic black-figure band-cup. The hero sets out on his impossible quest, armed by the gods.

images.alt: Perseus beheading Medusa, with Pegasus and Chrysaor springing from her blood.
images.caption: Birth of Pegasus — From Medusa's severed neck spring Pegasus and Chrysaor: beauty and terror born from blood.

images.alt: Medusa by Caravaggio, c. 1597. Uffizi Gallery, Florence.
images.caption: Medusa — Caravaggio, c. 1597. The moment of decapitation painted on a ceremonial shield: art imitating death.

images.alt: Odin by H. E. Freund, 1825–1827. Thorvaldsens Museum, Copenhagen.
images.caption: Odin — H. E. Freund, 1825–27. The All-Father stands in solemn power, spear Gungnir in hand, the source of Norse kingship.

images.alt: Detail of the statue Odin by Bengt Erland Fogelberg, Nationalmuseum, Stockholm.
images.caption: Odin of Fogelberg — Bengt Erland Fogelberg, 1830. Carrara marble capturing the lord of the gods with Huginn and Muninn on his helmet.

images.alt: Odin sacrificing himself upon Yggdrasil, modern illustration.
images.caption: Odin upon Yggdrasil — The god hangs from the World Tree for nine nights, spear-wounded, to seize the secret of the runes.

images.alt: Odin by Lorenz Frølich, 1844. Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen.
images.caption: Odin — Lorenz Frølich, 1844. The Danish master's vision of the one-eyed god in watercolor and ink.

images.alt: Wodan heals Baldr's horse by Emil Doepler, c. 1905.
images.caption: Wodan Heals Baldr's Horse — Emil Doepler, c. 1905. The All-Father as shaman and healer, wielding ancient Germanic magic.

images.alt: Valkyrie by Peter Nicolai Arbo, 1864. Nationalmuseum, Stockholm.
images.caption: Valkyrie — Peter Nicolai Arbo, 1864. One of Odin's choosers of the slain, riding through battlefields with spear and shield.

images.alt: Tor's Fight with the Giants by Mårten Eskil Winge, 1872. Nationalmuseum, Stockholm.
images.caption: Tor's Fight with the Giants — Mårten Eskil Winge, 1872. The thunder god in his chariot drawn by goats, hammer Mjölnir raised against the jötnar.

images.alt: Thor, der Donnergott by Johannes Gehrts, c. 1900.
images.caption: Thor, the Thunder God — Johannes Gehrts, c. 1900. The frontispiece to the Edda retold: red hair, lightning-wrapped hammer, belt of strength.

images.alt: Thor, Hymir and the Midgard Serpent, illustration from Teutonic Mythology, 1906.
images.caption: Thor Fishing for Jörmungandr — Illustration from Rydberg's Teutonic Mythology, 1906. The thunder god hooks the World Serpent, and the earth trembles.

images.alt: The Giant Skrymir and Thor by Louis Huard, 1900.
images.caption: Skrymir and Thor — Louis Huard, 1900. The giant UtgarÃ°a-Loki's servant towers over the thunder god in the land of illusions.

images.alt: Thor Destroys the Giant Thrym, illustration from Teutonic Mythology, 1906.
images.caption: Thor Destroys Thrym — Illustration from Rydberg's Teutonic Mythology, 1906. Mjölnir returns, and the giants fall.

images.alt: Ragnarök by Johannes Gehrts.
images.caption: Ragnarök — Johannes Gehrts. The final battle between the gods of Asgard and Loki's offspring: fire, flood, and the end of worlds.

images.alt: After Ragnarök by Emil Doepler, c. 1905.
images.caption: After Ragnarök — Emil Doepler, c. 1905. The world reborn from the ashes, green shoots rising over the sea.

images.alt: Surtr with the flaming sword by John Charles Dollman, 1909.
images.caption: Surtr — John Charles Dollman, 1909. The fire giant of Muspellheim raises his blazing sword to set the world aflame.

images.alt: Odin and Fenrir, Freyr and Surtr, illustration by Emil Doepler.
images.caption: The Death of Odin and Freyr — Emil Doepler. Odin falls to Fenrir's jaws; Freyr meets Surtr's flame. Two gods, two deaths, one doom.

images.alt: The binding of Fenrir by George Wright.
images.caption: The Binding of Fenrir — George Wright. The wolf who will one day break free and swallow the All-Father is chained by craft and courage.

images.alt: Shiva Nataraja, Chola bronze, c. 1100 CE. British Museum.
images.caption: Shiva Nataraja — Chola bronze, c. 1100 CE. The cosmic dancer: creation and destruction in a single gesture.

images.alt: Gudimallam Lingam, 2nd century BCE–1st century CE. Andhra Pradesh, India.
images.caption: Gudimallam Lingam — 2nd century BCE–1st century CE, Andhra Pradesh. The aniconic form of Shiva: raw generative power, without face or form.

images.alt: Shiva and Parvati as Uma-Maheshvara, red sandstone, Central India.
images.caption: Shiva and Parvati — Red sandstone Uma-Maheshvara from Central India. The divine couple united in eternal meditation.

images.alt: Ardhanarishvara, Chola period, 11th century CE. Government Museum, Chennai.
images.caption: Ardhanarishvara — Chola period, 11th century CE, Government Museum, Chennai. Half Shiva, half Parvati: the divine androgyny made stone.

images.alt: Shiva as Bhairava, Ellora Caves, Maharashtra.
images.caption: Bhairava — Ellora Caves, Maharashtra. The terrible form of Shiva: fangs, skulls, and the fire of annihilation.

images.alt: Standing Shiva Mahadeva, 8th century CE, Kashmir. Cleveland Museum of Art.
images.caption: Standing Shiva Mahadeva — 8th century CE, Kashmir. Cleveland Museum of Art. The ascetic god in calm, monumental power.

images.alt: Vishnu as Trivikrama, 7th century CE. Badami cave temple, Karnataka.
images.caption: Vishnu Trivikrama — 7th century CE, Badami cave temple. The dwarf Vamana who grew to stride across the universe in three steps.

images.alt: Anantasayana Vishnu, Chola granite, 11th century CE. Salar Jung Museum, Hyderabad.
images.caption: Vishnu Narayana — Chola granite, 11th century CE. The preserver reclines on the serpent Ananta, Lakshmi at his feet.

images.alt: Vishnu as Varaha, Udayagiri Caves, cave 5, c. 400 CE.
images.caption: Varaha Avatar — Udayagiri Caves, c. 400 CE. The boar-headed god lifts the earth goddess Bhudevi from the cosmic ocean.

images.alt: Krishna playing the flute, Pahari miniature, c. 1810–20. National Museum, New Delhi.
images.caption: Krishna — Pahari miniature, c. 1810–20. The most beloved avatar: flute-player, butter-thief, charioteer of Arjuna.

images.alt: Vishnu as Narasimha killing Hiranyakashipu, 12th century CE. Belur temple, Karnataka.
images.caption: Narasimha — 12th century CE, Belur. The man-lion avatar tears open the demon who thought himself immortal.

images.alt: Ganesha, Gupta period, c. 5th century CE. Government Museum, Mathura.
images.caption: Ganesha — Gupta period, c. 5th century CE, Mathura. The elephant-headed god of beginnings, remover of obstacles.

images.alt: Dancing Ganesha, bronze, c. 15th century CE. Indian Museum, Kolkata.
images.caption: Dancing Ganesha — Bronze, c. 15th century CE, Odisha. The god dances with a bowl of sweets, trunk curved in joy.

images.alt: Ganesha, Basohli miniature, c. 1730.
images.caption: Ganesha — Basohli miniature, c. 1730. The patron of arts and sciences, worshipped before every new venture.

images.alt: Stone sculpture of Ganesha. British Museum, London.
images.caption: Ganesha — Stone sculpture, British Museum. The most widely worshipped deity in the Hindu pantheon, beloved across India and beyond.

images.alt: Kali, Kalighat painting, 19th century. Cleveland Museum of Art.
images.caption: Kali — Kalighat painting, 19th century. The black goddess, tongue out in shock at her own violence, garlanded with skulls.

images.alt: Kali dancing on Shiva, Kalighat painting, 19th century. Cleveland Museum of Art.
images.caption: Dancing Kali — Kalighat painting, 19th century. The goddess dances on Shiva's body, time and destruction made flesh.

images.alt: Tantric form of Kali, folio from a book of iconography. LACMA.
images.caption: Kali Tantra — Folio from a book of iconography, LACMA. The fierce mother who destroys ego to liberate the soul.

images.alt: Kali Puja festival, modern devotional image.
images.caption: Kali — Modern devotional image. The divine mother who is simultaneously the most terrible and the most compassionate.

images.alt: Ra-Horakhty depicted as a falcon wearing the solar disk.
images.caption: Ra-Horakhty — Depicted as a falcon wearing the solar disk, the supreme sun god voyages across the sky.

images.alt: Ra-Horakhty statue, Rosicrucian Egyptian Museum.
images.caption: Ra-Horakhty — Rosicrucian Egyptian Museum. The falcon-headed sun god, protector of kings.

images.alt: Solar barque with Ra-Horakhty, tomb of Sennedjem.
images.caption: Ra in the Book of the Dead — Tomb of Sennedjem, c. 1275 BCE. The sun god in his barque travels through the underworld.

images.alt: Relief fragment of Akhenaten with the sun disk of the Aten.
images.caption: The Aten — Amarna period, c. 1350 BCE. Akhenaten's radiant sun disk, source of all life.

images.alt: Nun lifts the solar barque of Ra.
images.caption: The Solar Barque — Nun, god of chaos, lifts the barque of Ra into the sky at the dawn of time.

images.alt: Horus, Temple of Edfu, Egypt.
images.caption: Horus of Edfu — Temple of Edfu. The falcon-headed god, protector of kings, avenger of his father Osiris.

images.alt: Horus as falcon, Late Period Egypt.
images.caption: Horus the Falcon — Late Period statue. The god in his animal form: keen-eyed, swift, and terrible to his enemies.

images.alt: Wall relief of the battle between Horus and Seth, Temple of Edfu.
images.caption: Horus and Seth — Wall relief, Temple of Edfu. The eternal battle between order and chaos.

images.alt: Eye of Horus amulet.
images.caption: The Eye of Horus — Egyptian amulet. The wedjat eye: protection, royal power, and good health.

images.alt: Horus wearing the double crown of Upper and Lower Egypt.
images.caption: Horus Crowned — The double crown of Upper and Lower Egypt, symbolizing the unity Horus brought to the Two Lands.

images.alt: Heka, Egyptian god of magic, figurine.
images.caption: Heka — The personification of magic itself, the force that powered Egyptian religion and medicine.

images.alt: Graeco-Egyptian magical papyrus, Louvre.
images.caption: Heka in the Magical Papyrus — Graeco-Egyptian papyrus, Louvre. The word of power that opens doors and repels demons.

images.alt: Egyptian protective amulet of Taweret.
images.caption: Protective Amulet — Taweret amulet. Egyptian protective charm embodying heka to ward off evil.

images.alt: Menat necklace counterpoise with the heads of the deities Shu and Tefnut. Walters Art Museum.
images.caption: Menat with the Heads of Shu and Tefnut — A ritual counterpoise bearing the twin lion-deities of air and moisture. Walters Art Museum. Public domain via Wikimedia Commons.

images.alt: Reverse of the Menat with the heads of Shu and Tefnut. Walters Art Museum.
images.caption: Menat of Shu and Tefnut (reverse) — The reverse face of the same piece. Walters Art Museum. Public domain via Wikimedia Commons.

images.alt: Shu depicted with the ostrich feather of air upon his head.
images.caption: Shu with his Feather — The god of air crowned with the ostrich feather that is his name-sign. CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

images.alt: Sia, Egyptian god of perception.
images.caption: Sia — Personification of perception and understanding, attendant to Ra in his solar barque.

images.alt: Funerary papyrus from the Egyptian Book of the Dead.
images.caption: Sia in the Book of the Dead — Funerary papyrus, Louvre. The divine intelligence that guides the deceased.

images.alt: The Feather of Maat.
images.caption: The Feather of Maat — The ostrich feather, symbol of truth and the measure against which hearts are weighed.

images.alt: The Egyptian goddess Maat with feather of truth.
images.caption: Maat — The goddess of truth, justice, and cosmic order, wearing the feather of truth.

images.alt: Maat, Metropolitan Museum of Art.
images.caption: Maat — Metropolitan Museum of Art. The goddess kneels with outstretched wings, the embodiment of divine order.

images.alt: The Weighing of the Heart from the Book of the Dead of Ani.
images.caption: The Weighing of the Heart — Book of the Dead of Ani. The deceased's heart is weighed against Maat's feather.

images.alt: Akh iker en Re stela of Pahatia.
images.caption: The Akh — Stela of Pahatia, Museo Egizio, Turin. The transfigured spirit of the deceased, radiant in the afterlife.

images.alt: Akh iker en Re stela of Pahatia, detail.
images.caption: The Akh in the Presence of Ra — The blessed dead as an effective spirit, akh iker en Re.

images.alt: Egyptian heart scarab of Egyptian blue.
images.caption: The Heart (Ib/Ab) — Heart scarab of Egyptian blue. The seat of emotion, intellect, and morality in Egyptian belief.

images.alt: Anubis weighing the heart against the feather of Maat.
images.caption: The Heart in Judgement — Anubis weighs the heart against Maat's feather in the Hall of Judgement.

images.alt: The Ba as a bird with human head.
images.caption: The Ba — The personality and soul, depicted as a bird with a human head, free to fly between tomb and afterlife.

images.alt: Gold Ba bird amulet.
images.caption: Ba Bird Amulet — Gold amulet, Museo Egizio, Turin. The mobile aspect of the soul that could travel between worlds.

images.alt: The Ka hieroglyph of two upraised arms.
images.caption: The Ka Arms — The hieroglyph of two upraised arms: embrace, protection, the vital essence.

images.alt: Ka statue of King Hor, Egyptian Museum, Cairo.
images.caption: The Ka — Ka statue of King Hor, Egyptian Museum, Cairo. The life force, created at birth, sustained by offerings.

images.alt: Terracotta votary figurine from sanctuary of Astarte, Cyprus.
images.caption: Astarte Figurine — Terracotta votary from Kamelarga, Cyprus, c. 600–500 BCE. The goddess of fertility and power.

images.alt: Terracotta votary figurine from sanctuary of Astarte, Cyprus.
images.caption: Astarte at Kamelarga — Votary figurine from her sanctuary on Cyprus, bearer of life and desire.

images.alt: The Creation of the Sun, Moon and Plants by Michelangelo, 1508–1512. Sistine Chapel.
images.caption: The Primordial Void — Michelangelo, Sistine Chapel. Before light, before form: the chaos from which all emerged.

images.alt: Saturn Devouring His Son by Francisco Goya, c. 1823. Prado Museum.
images.caption: Saturn Devouring His Son — Goya, c. 1823. Chaos as primal terror: the father who consumes his children.

images.alt: Nike of Samothrace, c. 190 BCE. Louvre Museum, Paris.
images.caption: Nike of Samothrace — c. 190 BCE. The Winged Victory of Samothrace: power, motion, and triumph made marble.

images.alt: Nike by Paionios, c. 420 BCE. Archaeological Museum of Olympia.
images.caption: Nike by Paionios — c. 420 BCE. The goddess descends from Olympus to crown the victor, her wings spread wide.

images.alt: Nike adjusting her sandal, Temple of Athena Nike, c. 410 BCE. Acropolis Museum, Athens.
images.caption: Nike Adjusting Her Sandal — c. 410 BCE. The goddess in a moment of human intimacy, immortalized in marble.

images.alt: Earth from space, Apollo 17 Blue Marble.
images.caption: Gaia — Earth from space. The blue marble: the only world we know that breathes, thinks, and dreams.

images.alt: Tellus Mater relief from the Ara Pacis, Rome.
images.caption: Tellus Mater — Ara Pacis, Rome. The Roman earth-mother, fruit and grain in her lap, surrounded by wind and water.

images.alt: Psyche Revived by Cupid's Kiss by Antonio Canova, 1787. Louvre Museum.
images.caption: Psyche Revived by Cupid's Kiss — Antonio Canova, 1787. The moment love breathes life back into the soul.

images.alt: Eros Borghese, Roman copy. Louvre Museum.
images.caption: Eros Borghese — Roman copy, Louvre. The bow is bent, the arrow chosen: the god of desire as a beautiful youth.

images.alt: Sleeping Eros, Hellenistic bronze. Metropolitan Museum of Art.
images.caption: Sleeping Eros — Hellenistic bronze, Metropolitan Museum. The god of love at rest, his weapons forgotten, wings folded.

images.alt: Colossus of Rhodes, artistic reconstruction by Barclay.
images.caption: The Colossus of Rhodes — Voyage aux Sept Merveilles du Monde. The sun god straddling the harbor, one of the Seven Wonders.

images.alt: Helios in his quadriga, marble relief from Troy, c. 300–280 BCE.
images.caption: Helios in His Quadriga — Marble relief from Troy, c. 300–280 BCE. The sun god drives his four-horse chariot across the sky each dawn.

images.alt: Selene on her chariot, detail from a Roman sarcophagus. Metropolitan Museum of Art.
images.caption: Selene — Roman sarcophagus, Metropolitan Museum. The moon goddess descends in her chariot across the night sky.

images.alt: Selene and Endymion, Roman sarcophagus. Louvre Museum.
images.caption: Selene and Endymion — Roman sarcophagus, Louvre. The goddess descends to kiss her eternal sleeper.

images.alt: Vulcan (Hephaestus) by Guillaume II Coustou, 1742. Louvre Museum.
images.caption: Vulcan — Guillaume II Coustou, 1742, Louvre. The smith god, crippled but powerful, forge glowing behind him.

images.alt: The Forge of Vulcan by Diego Velázquez, 1630. Prado Museum.
images.caption: The Forge of Vulcan — Diego Velázquez, 1630. The god and his cyclopes hammering divine weapons.

images.alt: Hera Ludovisi, Roman copy. Palazzo Altemps, Rome.
images.caption: Hera Ludovisi — Roman copy, Palazzo Altemps. The queen of Olympus: regal, severe, and majestically beautiful.

images.alt: Hera Barberini, Roman copy. Vatican Museums.
images.caption: Hera Barberini — Vatican Museums. The goddess crowned and enthroned, the peacock at her feet.

images.alt: Hestia Giustiniani, Roman copy. Louvre Museum.
images.caption: Hestia Giustiniani — Louvre. The goddess of the hearth, veiled and serene.

images.alt: Temple of Vesta, Rome.
images.caption: Temple of Vesta — Rome. The eternal flame that must never be allowed to die.

images.alt: Farnese Atlas, Roman copy. National Archaeological Museum, Naples.
images.caption: Atlas Farnese — National Archaeological Museum, Naples. The Titan holds the celestial sphere, muscles straining under the weight of heaven.

images.alt: Farnese Atlas, another view. National Archaeological Museum, Naples.
images.caption: Atlas Farnese — Another view of the Titan bearing the heavens, the oldest surviving celestial globe.

images.alt: Hypnos and Thanatos carrying a dead warrior, Attic black-figure vase, c. 530 BCE. British Museum.
images.caption: Ker — Attic black-figure, c. 530 BCE. The winged death spirit carries the slain from the battlefield.

images.alt: Ruins of the ancient Spartan theatre, Greece.
images.caption: Ruins of Sparta — The city that feared neither death nor defeat, where boys were trained from age seven.

images.alt: Leonidas at Thermopylae by Jacques-Louis David, 1814.
images.caption: Leonidas at Thermopylae — Jacques-Louis David, 1814. The king who stood with 300 against an empire.

images.alt: Sunrise over the Black Sea (Pontos Euxeinos).
images.caption: The Black Sea — Pontos Euxeinos. The sea that gave its name to the primordial god of the deep.

images.alt: The Fall of the Rebel Angels by Pieter Bruegel the Elder, 1562. Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium.
images.caption: The Fall of the Rebel Angels — Bruegel, 1562. The Titans cast into Tartarus, falling through darkness eternal.

images.alt: Mount Olympus, Greece.
images.caption: Mount Olympus — The highest peak in Greece, home of the gods, throne of Zeus.

images.alt: The Tholos at Delphi, Greece.
images.caption: The Tholos at Delphi — The circular temple of Athena Pronaia, gateway to the oracle.

images.alt: Theater at Delphi, Greece.
images.caption: Theater at Delphi — Where the Pythian Games were held in honor of Apollo.

images.alt: The Acropolis of Athens.
images.caption: The Acropolis — Athens. The sacred rock: Parthenon, Erechtheion, Propylaea.

images.alt: The Parthenon, Athens.
images.caption: The Parthenon — The temple of Athena Parthenos, the most perfect building ever constructed.

images.alt: The Libyan Desert.
images.caption: The Libyan Desert — The vast Sahara that covers ancient Libya, land of Ammon and the oracle of Siwa.

images.alt: The Rape of Europa by Titian, 1560–1562. Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, Boston.
images.caption: The Rape of Europa — Titian, 1560–62. Zeus as a white bull carries the Phoenician princess across the sea.

images.alt: Satellite map of Europe.
images.caption: Europe — The continent that bears her name, from the Atlantic to the Urals.

images.alt: The Pyramids of Giza, Egypt.
images.caption: The Pyramids of Giza — The last surviving Wonder of the Ancient World, built for the pharaohs of the Fourth Dynasty.

images.alt: The Great Sphinx of Giza, Egypt.
images.caption: The Great Sphinx — Guardian of the necropolis, face of a pharaoh, body of a lion, watching eternity pass.

images.alt: Map of Asia Minor (Anatolia).
images.caption: Asia Minor — The land bridge between Europe and the ancient Near East.

images.alt: Hermod before Hela by John Charles Dollman, 1909.
images.caption: Hermod before Hela — John Charles Dollman, 1909. Odin's messenger kneels in the hall of the dead, begging for Baldr's return.

images.alt: Hel by Zarubina.
images.caption: Hel — Zarubina. The daughter of Loki, half living and half dead, enthroned in her underworld realm.

images.alt: Surtr with the flaming sword by John Charles Dollman, 1909.
images.caption: Surtr in Muspellheim — John Charles Dollman, 1909. The fire giant waits with his blazing sword to burn the world at Ragnarök.

images.alt: The Nine Worlds of Norse Religion.
images.caption: The Nine Worlds — Midgard at the center of the cosmos, home of humankind, encircled by Jörmungandr and joined to the other realms by Yggdrasil.

images.alt: Dancing Fairies by August Malmström. Nationalmuseum, Stockholm.
images.caption: Alfheim — August Malmström, Dancing Fairies. The realm of the light elves: luminous, graceful, and forever dancing at the edge of mortal sight.

images.alt: The Giant Skrymir and Thor by Louis Huard, 1900.
images.caption: Jötunheimr — Louis Huard, 1900. The land of giants: Skrymir, servant of UtgarÃ°a-Loki, towers over Thor in the realm of ancient enmity.

images.alt: Kobe, Japan, at night.
images.caption: Kobe — The port city between mountains and sea, famous for its beef and its resilience.

images.alt: Fushimi Inari Shrine, Kyoto, Japan.
images.caption: Fushimi Inari Shrine — Kyoto. Thousands of vermillion torii gates winding up the mountain.

images.alt: Kinkaku-ji (Golden Pavilion), Kyoto, Japan.
images.caption: Kinkaku-ji — The Golden Pavilion, reflected in its mirror pond, the most photographed temple in Japan.

images.alt: Osaka Castle, Japan.
images.caption: Osaka Castle — The fortress of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, rebuilt in concrete and gold, symbol of Japanese unification.

images.alt: Brahma (Prajapati) emerging from a lotus growing from Vishnu's navel, 1913 illustration.
images.caption: Prajapati — The Lord of Creatures, shown as Brahma emerging from the cosmic lotus. The primordial creator from whom all beings emanate.

images.alt: Vedic yajna fire altar, Howrah, 2012.
images.caption: Vedic Fire Altar — The ritual fire (Agni) maintained in perfect order, embodying á¹šta, the cosmic law that governs gods and mortals alike.

images.caption: Aether battles the lion-headed Giant Leon on the Gigantomachy frieze of the Pergamon Altar, first half of the 2nd century BC. Pergamon Museum, Berlin. Photo by Carlos Gonzalez, 2013.

images.alt: Loki Patera Color Voyager
images.caption: Loki Patera Color Voyager — A huge area of Io's volcanic plains is shown in this Voyager 1 image mosaic. Numerous volcanic calderas and lava flows are visible here. Loki Patera, an active lava lake, is the large shield-shaped black feature. Heat emitted from Loki can be seen through telescopes all the way from Earth. These telescopic observations tell us that Loki has been active continuously (or at least every time astronomers have looked) since the Voyager 1 flyby in March 1979. The composition of Io's volcanic plains and lava flows has not been determined, but they could consist dominantly of sulfur with surface frosts of sulfur dioxide or of silicates (such as basalts) encrusted with sulfur and sulfur dioxide condensates. The bright whitish patches probably consist of freshly deposited SO2 frost. The black spots, including Loki, are probably hot sulfur lava, which may remain molten by intrusions of molten silicate magma, coming up from deeper within Io. The ultimate source of heat that keeps Io active is tidal frictional heating due to the continual flexure of Io by the gravity of Jupiter and Europa, another of Jupiter's satellites. (NASA/JPL/USGS, Public domain)

images.alt: Scandinavia.TMO2003050
images.caption: Scandinavia.TMO2003050 — Scandinavia from space in winter. The Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) instrument aboard NASA’s Terra satellite captured the above image of the Scandinavian Peninsula on February 19, 2003. With a landscape largely shaped by glaciers over the last ice age, the Scandinavian Peninsula is as picturesque in the winter as it is cold. Along the left side of the peninsula, one can see the jagged inlets, known as fjords, lining Norway’s coast. Many of these fjords are well over 2,000 feet (610 meters) deep and were carved out by extremely heavy, thick glaciers that formed during the last ice age. The glaciers ran off the mountains and scoured troughs into Norway’s coastline with depths that reached well below sea level. When the glaciers melted, the seawater rushed into these deep troughs to form the fjords. The deepest fjord on Norway’s coast, known as Sogn Fjord, lies in southwest Norway and is 4,291 feet (1,308 m) deep. Glaciers also carved the mountains in Norway and northernmost Sweden. South of this mountainous region, however, Sweden consists mostly of flat, heavily forested land dotted with lakes. Lake Vänern and Lake Vättern, the largest of Sweden’s lakes, do not freeze completely during the winter months and can be seen clearly at the bottom of the peninsula. Lake Vättern, the smaller of the two lakes, was connected to the Baltic Sea during the last ice age. After the ice melted, a tremendous weight was lifted off of the peninsula, and the landmass rose up to separate the lake from the Baltic Sea. To the northeast of the peninsula lies Finland with more than 55,000 lakes, most of which were also created by glacial deposits. (Jacques Descloitres, MODIS Land Rapid Response Team at NASA GSFC, Public domain)

images.alt: Satellite image of Madagascar in September 2003
images.caption: Satellite image of Madagascar in September 2003 — Satellite image of Madagascar in September 2003. Slightly cropped, original taken from NASA's Visible Earth: [1] . Original description: The world's fourth largest island, Madagascar, is featured in this Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) image taken by the Terra satellite on September 10, 2003. Several active fires, marked with red dots, burn in the central highlands, which are primarily covered with rice fields. The fires are probably controlled burns to clear farmland. The narrow strip of green along the east coast of the island is a rain forest. The west coast is lined with baobabs, a desert tree with a fat trunk, and thorny forest. (Unknown author Unknown author, Public domain)

images.alt: Satellite image of France in August 2002
images.caption: Satellite image of France in August 2002 — Satellite image of France acquired August 14, 2002, by the Terra satellite. An unusually cloud-free France shows green and tan in this true-color Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) image acquired August 14, 2002, by the Terra satellite. The great city of Paris is visible in the upper center of the image as a gray smudge against the landscape, and is even clearer in the higher resolutions of this image. To the north, clouds mostly obscure the English Channel, but the Bay of Biscay to the west is clear, as is the Mediterranean Sea to the south. The northernmost portion of Spain is clearly visible at the bottom of the image, and is separated from France by the Pyrenees Mountain Range. (Jacques Descloitres, MODIS Rapid Response Team, NASA/GSFC, Public domain)

images.alt: Satellite image of New Zealand in December 2002
images.caption: Satellite image of New Zealand in December 2002 — Satellite image of New Zealand in December 2002. NASA's description: These stunning true-color images provide a rare, cloud-free look at the island nation of New Zealand, including most of its North and South Islands. This scene was acquired by the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS), flying aboard NASA’s Terra satellite, on October 23, and December 31, 2002. New Zealand is situated in the South Pacific Ocean, roughly 2,000 km (1,250 miles) southeast of Australia. Wellington, the capital of New Zealand, is located on the southern tip of the North Island, looking across Cook Strait toward South Island. (Jacques Descloitres, MODIS Land Rapid Response Team at NASA GSFC, Public domain)

Dennis 2005-07-07 1550Z — Hurricane Dennis threaded its way between Jamaica and Haiti on a direct course for Cuba on July 7, 2005. The storm now has the distinctive hurricane form, with a well-defined eye surrounded by bands of swirling clouds. At 10:50 a.m. local time (15:50 UTC), when the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) on NASA's Terra satellite took this image, Dennis was just below a Category 3 hurricane, with winds of 175 kilometers per hour (110 miles per hour) and stronger gusts. Less than an hour before this image was taken, the storm's small dark eye was about 105 kilometers (65 miles) northeast of Kingston, Jamaica, and 170 kilometers (105 miles) south-southeast of Guantanamo, Cuba. The National Hurricane Center reports that Dennis is traveling northwest at about 24 kilometers per hour (15 mph). A storm of this size is a threat not just because of its powerful winds: Dennis is expected to produce heavy rain and coastal and inland flooding. Five to ten inches of rain may fall over Haiti, the Dominican Republic, Jamaica, Cuba, and the Cayman Islands, with as much as 15 inches falling in parts of Jamaica. Heavy rainfall can trigger flash floods and mudslides in mountainous regions. The storm will probably also raise tide levels by five to seven feet and generate large and dangerous waves. Dennis is expected to strengthen as it moves north towards the Gulf Coast of the United States. For official storm warnings and additional information, please visit the National Hurricane Center. The image is available in additional resolutions from the MODIS Rapid Response Team. (NASA image courtesy Jeff Schmaltz, MODIS Land Rapid Response Team at NASA GSFC, Public domain)

images.alt: Antarctica 6400px from Blue Marble
images.caption: Antarctica 6400px from Blue Marble — Antarctica . An orthographic projection of NASA's Blue Marble data set (1 km resolution global satellite composite). "MODIS observations of polar sea ice were combined with observations of Antarctica made by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s AVHRR sensor—the Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer." Image was generated using a custom C program for handling the Blue Marble files, with orthographic projection formulas from MathWorld . Note: this image has been manually modified to fill in an area of black pixels in the ocean, in the upper right quadrant. The black pixels are presumed to be due to missing data in the land/sea mask used in making the original Blue Marble image. (Dave Pape, Public domain)

images.alt: A cylinder seal from Mari with a divine scene of order and chaos
images.caption: A cylinder seal from Mari with a divine scene of order and chaos — A cylinder seal found in Mari on the middle Euphrates, dates 2340–2159 BC. El holds a scepter (which characterizes him as the king of gods) and is enthroned on a mountain that reaches the sky (as attested by the stars near it). From both sides of the mountain, rivers flow out of two animal protomes (in Ugarit, El is described dwelling in mbk nhrm qrb apq thmtm – "the springs of the Double-Rivers, Amidst the channels of the Double-Deeps" (translation: Mark S. Smith, The Ugaritic Baal Cycle vol. 1, Brill, 1994, p. 218) ). Two tree-goddesses are standing by his sides, emerging from the river; one holds a tree, the other holds a vessel. Another god, of the type of Baal-Hadad, fights the flood (interpreted as Yam, god of the and the rivers, of Leviathan- ltn , his servant) with a spear. The water, that allows the trees to grow, can also be threatening and destructive. This copy of the impression of the seal was made by pencils. (פעמי-עליון, CC BY-SA 4.0)

images.alt: Descent of Phoenix with a crater in the background taken by Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter
images.caption: Descent of Phoenix with a crater in the background taken by Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter — Image taken by Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter showing descent of Phoenix with a crater in the background. Original caption from NASA: "Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter's High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) camera acquired this image of Phoenix hanging from its parachute as it descended to the Martian surface. Shown here is a 10 kilometer (6 mile) diameter crater informally called "Heimdall," and an improved full-resolution image of the parachute and lander. Although it appears that Phoenix is descending into the crater, it is actually about 20 kilometers (about 12 miles) in front of the crater. Given the position and pointing angle of MRO, Phoenix is at about 13 km above the surface, just a few seconds after the parachute opened. This image shows some details of the parachute, including the gap between upper and lower sections. At the time of this observation, MRO had an orbital altitude of 310 km, traveling at a ground velocity of 3.4 kilometers/second, and a distance of 760 km to the Phoenix lander. The Phoenix Mission is led by the University of Arizona, Tucson, on behalf of NASA. Project management of the mission is by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, Calif. Spacecraft development is by Lockheed Martin Space Systems, Denver." (NASA/Jet Propulsion Lab-Caltech/University of Arizona, Public domain)

images.alt: Pan and Daphnis, marble group. National Archaeological Museum, Naples.
images.caption: Pan and Daphnis — Roman copy of a Hellenistic original by Heliodoros of Rhodes, Inv. 6329. The goat-legged god leans in to teach the shepherd boy the pipes, desire folded into the gift of music itself.

images.alt: Nicolas Poussin, The Triumph of Pan, 1636. National Gallery, London.
images.caption: The Triumph of Pan — Nicolas Poussin, 1636. Around the god's term and his sacred tortoise, Arcadia erupts into dance: the wild made stately, the rite made eternal.

images.alt: Pan and Hermaphroditus, Roman fresco from the House of the Dioscuri, Pompeii. Naples Museum.
images.caption: Pan and Hermaphroditus — fresco from the House of the Dioscuri, Pompeii. The shaggy god of the lonely hillsides steps into a Roman dining room, as playful and uninvited as panic itself.

images.alt: Marble votive relief of Pan, Hermes and the Nymphs, c. 360 BC, from the Cave of the Nymphs, Mount Penteli. National Archaeological Museum, Athens.
images.caption: Votive Relief of Pan, Hermes and the Nymphs — c. 360 BC, dedicated in the Cave of the Nymphs on Mount Penteli. Carved at his own sanctuary, Pan sits piping beside the cave mouth where the Athenians swore he danced with the nymphs.

images.alt: Apulian red-figure bell krater with Pan holding syrinx and lagobolon, mid-4th century BC. Musei Capitolini, Rome.
images.caption: Apulian Red-Figure Bell Krater — mid-4th century BC, Musei Capitolini. Pan appears with his two signatures, the syrinx and the hunting-stick: the musician and the goatherd who owns the noonday hush.

images.alt: Marco Dente after Raphael, Pan and Syrinx, engraving, c. 1516. Kupferstichkabinett, Berlin.
images.caption: Pan and Syrinx — engraving by Marco Dente da Ravenna after a design attributed to Raphael, c. 1516. The Renaissance restages the chase that ends in metamorphosis: the nymph becomes reeds, and the reeds become the god's first song.

images.alt: Chimera of Arezzo, Etruscan bronze, c. 400 BC. Museo Archeologico Nazionale, Florence.
images.caption: Chimera of Arezzo — Etruscan bronze, c. 400 BC, unearthed in 1553. Wounded but unconquered, the lion-bodied monster twists against Bellerophon's blow, her goat head still hissing defiance — a votive gift inscribed TINSCVIL to the sky-god Tin. Museo Archeologico Nazionale, Florence.

images.alt: Attic red-figure pelike, Bellerophon on Pegasus fighting the Chimera, c. 440 BC. Louvre G535.
images.caption: Pelike G535 — Attic red-figure pelike, c. 440 BC. Bellerophon leans from Pegasus' back to drive his spear into the Chimaira, the moment Greek painters chose again and again: the impossible beast made killable. Louvre, Paris.

images.alt: Middle Corinthian plate by the Chimaera Painter depicting the Chimaira, c. 600–570 BC. Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna.
images.caption: Chimaera Painter plate — Middle Corinthian, c. 600–570 BC. On the painter's own name-piece the Chimaira stands alone in heraldic splendor, lion foreparts and serpent tail coiled into one of the earliest surviving portraits of the monster. Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna.

images.alt: Frieze slabs from the Heroon of Trysa showing Bellerophon against the Chimera, c. 380 BC. Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna.
images.caption: Heroon of Trysa frieze — Lycian tomb frieze, c. 380 BC. On the inner wall of the great Gjølbaşı heroon, Bellerophon charges the Chimaira in marble — the myth carved at the very edge of Lycia, where legend first set the fire-breathing mountain. Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna.

images.alt: Attic black-figure neck amphora by the Bellerophon Painter, Bellerophon on Pegasus and the Chimaira, c. 575–550 BC. Athens NM 16391.
images.caption: Bellerophon Painter name vase — Attic black-figure neck amphora, c. 575–550 BC. The painter took his modern name from this very scene: Pegasus rears above the crouching Chimaira as the spear falls, Archaic Athens' crisp telling of the labors of Lycia. National Archaeological Museum, Athens.

images.alt: Apulian red-figure oinochoe attributed to the Felton Painter, Bellerophon slaying the Chimaera, second quarter 4th century BC. Taranto, MARTA 52363.
images.caption: Apulian oinochoe, Felton Painter — red-figure, second quarter of the 4th century BC. Magna Graecia's lush retelling: Bellerophon and Pegasus close over the fallen Chimaera, her leonine body already folding beneath the hero's lance. MARTA, Taranto.

images.alt: Chimera of Arezzo, second view in the Sala dei Bronzi, Museo Archeologico Nazionale, Florence.
images.caption: Chimera of Arezzo, Sala dei Bronzi — the full profile of the votive bronze: serpent-tail rearing to strike back, goat-neck torn open by the hero's wound, proof that even Etruscan craftsmen rendered the monster's agony without ever granting her defeat. Museo Archeologico Nazionale, Florence.

images.alt: Marble metope of Helios in his quadriga rising from the sea, Temple of Athena at Ilion, 300–280 BC. Altes Museum, Berlin.
images.caption: The Helios Metope of Troy — from the Temple of Athena at Ilion, 300–280 BC: the sun god bursts from the sea in his quadriga, head ringed by a rayed halo — the definitive ancient image of the chariot of Hyperion's house.

images.alt: Attic black-figure lekythos by the Sappho Painter, ca. 500 BC, showing Helios rising in his chariot between Nyx and Eos. Metropolitan Museum of Art.
images.caption: Sappho Painter Lekythos — Attic black-figure, ca. 500 BC: Helios rises in his four-horse chariot between Nyx departing and Eos awakening, the Titan's daily circuit painted at the very moment of dawn.

images.alt: Horses of Helios's chariot rising from Okeanos, left corner of the east pediment of the Parthenon, 438–432 BC. British Museum, London.
images.caption: East Pediment of the Parthenon — Phidias's workshop, 438–432 BC: at the left corner the horses of Helios rear out of the waters of Okeanos, the sun-god pediment that framed the birth of Athena with the Titan's rising light.

images.alt: Philips Galle after Maarten van Heemskerck, Colossus Solis, engraving of 1572 imagining the bronze Colossus of Rhodes astride the harbor. Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam.
images.caption: Colossus Solis — Philips Galle after Maarten van Heemskerck, 1572: the Renaissance's great imagining of the bronze Colossus of Rhodes, the seventy-cubit statue of the sun god that stood as the Wonder of Hyperion's cult.

images.alt: Roman relief from the theatre of Perge showing Helios in a quadriga attacking the Giants, with Oceanos, Tethys and Eos. Antalya Museum.
images.caption: Gigantomachy of Perge — Roman relief from the theatre of Perge, Antalya Museum: Helios drives his quadriga into the battle of gods and Giants while Oceanos and Tethys surge beside him and Eos runs before the horses.

images.alt: Late antique floor mosaic in the Hammat Tiberias synagogue: Helios in his chariot at the center of the zodiac wheel.
images.caption: Hammat Tiberias Zodiac Mosaic — synagogue floor of late antiquity: crowned with rays and driving his chariot, Helios holds the center of the turning zodiac, the old sun god still ordering the wheel of the year.

images.alt: Marble statue of Clio holding a scroll, Museo Pio-Clementino, Vatican Museums.
images.caption: Clio, Museo Pio-Clementino (Inv. 291) — Roman marble of the 2nd century CE from the Villa of Cassius near Tivoli: the Muse of History stands in the Vatican's Hall of the Muses, scroll in hand, her head a non-pertinent ancient restoration.

images.alt: Relief of Clio holding writing tablets, detail of the Muses Sarcophagus, Louvre.
images.caption: The Muses Sarcophagus, Louvre (Ma 475) — a marble sarcophagus of the early 2nd century AD found by the Via Ostiense, where Kleiṓ appears with her writing tablets, recording memory among her eight sisters.

images.alt: Tessellated portrait of Clio from the Vichten mosaic, c. 240 AD, National Museum of History and Art, Luxembourg.
images.caption: The Vichten Mosaic, c. 240 AD — from a Roman villa in Gallia Belgica and now in Luxembourg's National Museum of History and Art, this tessellated Kleiṓ presides over the Nine Muses' cycle, diptych in hand.

images.alt: Clio panel from the Mosaic of the Nine Muses from Kos, Grand Master's Palace, Rhodes.
images.caption: The Nine Muses Mosaic from Kos — a Roman-era floor recovered on Kos and set today in the Grand Master's Palace in Rhodes, portraying Kleiṓ with the scroll that marks her domain over recorded time.

images.alt: Seated Roman statue of Clio from Hadrian's Villa, Museo del Prado, Madrid.
images.caption: Clio from Hadrian's Villa (Prado E-68) — a Roman marble of 130–150 AD unearthed at the emperor's Tivoli retreat, showing the Muse enthroned, the historian's composure carved in stone.

images.alt: Charles Meynier, Clio, Muse of History, oil on canvas, Cleveland Museum of Art.
images.caption: Charles Meynier, Clio, Muse of History (1800) — the Neoclassical canvas at the Cleveland Museum of Art crowns the Muse with laurel as she writes the deeds of ages into her great book.

images.alt: Artemisia Gentileschi, Clio, 1632, oil on canvas.
images.caption: Artemisia Gentileschi, Clio (1632) — the Baroque master's Muse of History turns from her open book, trumpet at hand, ready to proclaim the fame her pages preserve.

images.alt: Circe Offering the Cup to Ulysses by John William Waterhouse, 1891. Gallery Oldham.
images.caption: Circe Offering the Cup to Ulysses — Waterhouse's 1891 masterpiece: the enchantress of Aiaia enthroned, raising the drugged bowl while a transformed sailor grunts at her feet and Odysseus looms in her mirror.

images.alt: Attic black-figure kylix by the Painter of the Boston Polyphemos, ca. 560–550 BCE, showing Circe's victims. Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
images.caption: Boston kylix of the Painter of the Boston Polyphemos — Attic black-figure wine cup, ca. 560–550 BCE (MFA 99.518): Circe's potion mid-work, Odysseus' men half beast and half man — the earliest surviving image of the witch at her craft. Photo: Lucas / ancientartpodcast, CC BY 2.0.

images.alt: Circe Invidiosa by John William Waterhouse, 1892. Art Gallery of South Australia, Adelaide.
images.caption: Circe Invidiosa — Waterhouse's 1892 Ovidian vision: jealous Circe poisons the well where her rival Scylla will bathe, the venom glowing green at her toes.

images.alt: Arula, small terracotta altar with a relief of Circe transforming Odysseus' man, 6th century BCE. Louvre, CA 5956.
images.caption: Arula of Kirke — a polychrome terracotta altar from Sicily, third quarter of the 6th century BCE (Louvre CA 5956): on its side panel Circe works the shapeshifting of Odysseus' companion, among the oldest named images of the goddess.

images.alt: Ulysses and Circe by Bartholomeus Spranger, c. 1586–1587. Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna.
images.caption: Ulysses and Circe — Bartholomeus Spranger's Mannerist panel, c. 1586–87 (Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna): the hero, proofed by Hermes' moly, confronts a Circe whose spell is failing in mid-gesture.

images.alt: Circe Mulling Wine by Gioacchino Assereto, c. 1630. Dayton Art Institute.
images.caption: Circe Mulling Wine — Gioacchino Assereto's Baroque enchantress, c. 1630 (Dayton Art Institute): she broods over the cup, the alchemy of the isle distilled to a single dark thought.

images.alt: Circe by Wright Barker, 1889, standing with her wand among lions, wolves, and foxes.
images.caption: Circe — Wright Barker's 1889 portrait: wand in hand, ringed by lions, wolves, and foxes — the men she has remade in animal form, kept as her court on Aiaia.

images.alt: Ōnamuchi no Mikoto, oil painting by Aoki Shigeru, Ishibashi Museum of Art.
images.caption: Ōnamuchi no Mikoto — Aoki Shigeru's great Meiji canvas (Ishibashi Museum of Art, Kurume). Slain by his eighty brothers, the lord of Izumo lies in the grass while the two shell-goddesses sent by Kamimusubi anoint him with clam milk — the Kojiki's resurrection of the land-builder, painted at the height of Japan's Western-style art.

images.alt: Prince Okuni and a Hare, surimono woodblock print by Yashima Gakutei, c. 1819. Metropolitan Museum of Art.
images.caption: Prince Okuni and a Hare — Yashima Gakutei, surimono, probably 1819 (Metropolitan Museum of Art). The white-haired god of Izumo stands in chrysanthemum-patterned robes on a rocky shore, the White Hare of Inaba crouched at his feet — the little prophet whose blessing made Ōkuninushi master of the Central Land of Reed-Plains.

images.alt: Ōnamuchi from the Shinbutsu-zue, Edo-period illustrated compendium of kami and buddhas.
images.caption: Ōnamuchi from the Shinbutsu-zue — Edo-period woodblock compendium of the kami and buddhas. Haloed and staff in hand, the god sits beneath a litany of his seven names — Ōkuninushi, Ōnamuchi, Ōmononushi — the standard early-modern icon of the deity who built and then yielded Japan's heartland.

images.alt: Bronze statues of Ōkuninushi and the white rabbit at Jishu Shrine, Kyoto.
images.caption: Bronze of Ōkuninushi and the White Rabbit — Jishu Shrine, Kyoto's famed shrine of love-matches. Mallet raised, the god of nation-building stands beside the hare he healed at Cape Keta — the act of kindness that won him a kingdom, cast in bronze where couples still pray for en-musubi, the tying of fates.

images.alt: Ōkuninushi and the field mouse, Meiji-period book illustration, 1911.
images.caption: Ōkuninushi and the Field Mouse — Meiji-era book illustration, 1911. Amid the burning meadow of Susano-o's cruelest trial, a field mouse leads the god to a burrow and returns his arrow — the Kojiki's proof that the smallest ally can undo a storm-god's trap.

images.alt: Ōkuninushi asks the toad, book illustration from Izumo Shinwa, 1938.
images.caption: Ōkuninushi asks the toad — illustration from Izumo Shinwa, 1938. The god points across the water at a tiny approaching craft while the toad names its rider — Sukunabikona, the dwarf god come in a kagami-bune to help Ōkuninushi finish building the land.

images.alt: Bronze swords and spears from the Kōjindani cache, Yayoi period, displayed at the Shimane Museum of Ancient Izumo.
images.caption: The Kōjindani bronze cache — Shimane Museum of Ancient Izumo. Three hundred fifty-eight bronze swords, spears and bells buried in ritual order in Yayoi-period Izumo — the unearthed arsenal of the ancient land Ōkuninushi ruled, and by his own word surrendered to the heavenly sun-line.

images.alt: Priestess of Delphi, by John Collier (1891): the Pythia standing over her tripod with laurel.
images.caption: Priestess of Delphi (John Collier, 1891) — the Pythia stands above her tripod, laurel bough and sacred smoke in hand, the living voice of the oracular seat Phoebe once held at Delphi.

images.alt: Attic red-figure kylix by the Kodros Painter (c. 440–430 BC): King Aegeus consults the oracle at Delphi.
images.caption: The Delphic Oracle — Attic red-figure kylix by the Kodros Painter, c. 440–430 BC: King Aegeus stands before the enthroned figure on the oracular tripod, the earliest surviving image of prophecy spoken at Phoebe's Delphi.

images.alt: The Oracle, by Camillo Miola (1880): the Pythia convulsed upon the tripod between temple columns. J. Paul Getty Museum.
images.caption: The Oracle (Camillo Miola, 1880) — the Pythia writhes upon the great tripod between the columns of Apollo's temple while the priests bear witness, the trance of divine utterance rendered in marble light.

images.alt: Consulting the Oracle, by John William Waterhouse (1884): suppliants gathered around the priestess. Tate Britain.
images.caption: Consulting the Oracle (John William Waterhouse, 1884) — a circle of petitioners leans toward the priestess of Delphi, each waiting on the few god-sent words that will govern a life.

images.alt: Lycurgus Consulting the Pythia, attributed to Eugène Delacroix: the Spartan lawgiver before the enthroned priestess.
images.caption: Lycurgus Consulting the Pythia (attributed to Eugène Delacroix) — the Spartan lawgiver kneels to receive his laws from the enthroned priestess, Delphi's authority over the whole Greek world made visible.

images.alt: Marble omphalos carved with a woollen net, Delphi Archaeological Museum.
images.caption: The Omphalos — the marble navel-stone of Delphi, carved with its woollen net (Delphi Archaeological Museum): the very centre of the world, where Phoebe held the oracle before bequeathing it to her grandson Apollo.

images.alt: Doric columns of the Temple of Apollo at Delphi against the slopes of Mount Parnassus.
images.caption: The Temple of Apollo at Delphi — the re-erected Doric columns still stand against the slopes of Parnassus, the house of the oracle that Earth gave to Themis, Themis to Phoebe, and Phoebe to Phoebus Apollo.

images.alt: Tondo of an Attic black-figure kylix inscribed with the name Eris. Antikensammlung Berlin, F 1775.
images.caption: Attic black-figure kylix, inscribed Eris — the sole surviving vase to name the goddess herself: Eris strides through the tondo of a lip cup painted between 575 and 525 BC, her identity fixed by the painter's own inscription (Antikensammlung Berlin, F 1775; LIMC Eris 1).

images.alt: J. M. W. Turner, The Goddess of Discord Choosing the Apple of Contention in the Garden of the Hesperides, c. 1806. Tate Britain, London.
images.caption: The Goddess of Discord Choosing the Apple of Contention in the Garden of the Hesperides — J. M. W. Turner's c. 1806 epic (Tate Britain) gives Eris her rare starring canvas, plucking the fatal apple among the Hesperides' dragon-guarded boughs before the whole Trojan War unfolds from her hand.

images.alt: Jacob Jordaens, The Wedding of Thetis and Peleus — The Golden Apple of Discord. Museo del Prado, Madrid.
images.caption: The Golden Apple of Discord (The Wedding of Thetis and Peleus) — Jacob Jordaens's Prado banquet scene catches the precise instant of ruin: uninvited Eris hurls the golden apple into the feast of the gods, the seed from which the Judgment of Paris and the war at Troy will grow.

images.alt: Peter Paul Rubens, The Judgement of Paris, c. 1606. Museo del Prado, Madrid.
images.caption: The Judgement of Paris — Rubens's c. 1606 Prado canvas stages the harvest of Eris's apple: Hermes leads Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite before the Trojan shepherd, whose verdict for love over wisdom and power kindles ten years of war.

images.alt: Lucas Cranach the Elder, The Judgement of Paris, 1528. Kunstmuseum Basel.
images.caption: The Judgement of Paris, 1528 — Lucas Cranach the Elder's signed and dated panel (Kunstmuseum Basel) recasts the Trojan prince as a dreaming knight in armor, the three goddesses arriving to claim the apple Eris set among them.

images.alt: Marcantonio Raimondi after Raphael, The Judgment of Paris, engraving, c. 1510–1520. National Gallery of Art, Washington.
images.caption: The Judgment of Paris (engraving after Raphael) — Marcantonio Raimondi's celebrated c. 1510–1520 print spreads Eris's quarrel across the Renaissance world, engraving the moment three rival goddesses submit their beauty to a mortal's disastrous choice.

images.alt: Antoine Watteau, The Judgement of Paris, 1718–1721. Musée du Louvre, Paris.
images.caption: The Judgement of Paris — Antoine Watteau's 1718–1721 Louvre panel distills the myth into Rococo intimacy: Paris extends the golden apple toward Aphrodite while Cupid clings to her, closing the circuit Eris opened at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis.

images.alt: Thalia holding a comic mask, detail of the Muses Sarcophagus. Louvre, Paris.
images.caption: The Muses Sarcophagus — marble, first half of the 2nd century AD, found by the Via Ostiense (Louvre, Ma 475): Thaleia lifts the grinning comic mask, her attribute among the nine Muses and the oldest smile in the canon of comedy.

images.alt: Seated marble statue of Thalia from the Villa of Cassius at Tivoli. Vatican Museums.
images.caption: The Tivoli Thalia — Hadrianic marble (AD 117–138) from the Villa of Cassius near Tivoli, now in the Hall of the Muses, Museo Pio-Clementino: the Muse of comedy sits crowned in ivy, the theatre mask resting at her side.

images.alt: Thalia detail of the Vichten mosaic of the nine Muses, c. 240 AD. National Museum of History and Art, Luxembourg.
images.caption: The Vichten Mosaic — Roman floor mosaic, c. 240 AD (National Museum of History and Art, Luxembourg): among the nine Muses in their hexagonal panels, Thaleia appears with her comic mask, laughter set in stone for a Gallo-Roman villa.

images.alt: Marble statue of Thalia with a pedum, Roman period. British Museum, London.
images.caption: The British Museum Thalia — Roman marble in chiton and himation (British Museum, London): the Muse stands with the pedum, the shepherd's crook of idyllic poetry, her drapery carved thin as laughter's disguise.

images.alt: Silver denarius of Q. Pomponius Musa, 56 BC, showing Thalia with a comic mask.
images.caption: Denarius of Quintus Pomponius Musa — Rome, 56 BC: the moneyer's pun on his own name puts Thaleia on silver, standing in flowing peplos with the comic mask in hand — comedy's Muse minted into daily currency.

images.alt: Hendrick Goltzius, engraving of Thalia, the Muse of Comedy. Metropolitan Museum of Art.
images.caption: Goltzius's Thalia — Hendrick Goltzius, engraving, 1592 (Metropolitan Museum of Art): the Northern Mannerist burin gives the ancient Muse a Baroque swagger, mask and trumpet in hand, as comedy steps into the print culture of a new age.

images.alt: Botticelli, Primavera (detail): Zephyr seizing Chloris. Uffizi, Florence.
images.caption: Primavera — Zephyr and Chloris — Botticelli, c. 1482, Uffizi: the blue-grey west wind bursts through the dark wood to seize the nymph Chloris, flowers already spilling from her lips as Ovid's rape turns to marriage mid-gust.

images.alt: Botticelli, The Birth of Venus (detail): Zephyr and Chloris blowing Venus ashore. Uffizi, Florence.
images.caption: The Birth of Venus — Zephyr and Chloris — Botticelli, c. 1485, Uffizi: locked in his consort's arms, the west wind blows the newborn goddess to shore on a soft, rose-bearing breath — the gentlest face of Zephyros ever painted.

images.alt: Marble relief of Zephyrus, frieze of the Tower of the Winds, Roman Agora, Athens.
images.caption: Zephyrus on the Tower of the Winds — marble frieze of the Horologion of Andronikos Kyrrhestes, Athens, c. 100–50 BC: among the eight sculpted winds, the westerly one flies as a bare-limbed youth, his cloak brimming with the flowers of spring he scatters.

images.alt: Attic red-figure kylix, manner of Douris: Zephyrus and Hyakinthos. Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
images.caption: Zephyrus and Hyakinthos — Attic red-figure kylix from Tarquinia, manner of Douris, c. 490–485 BC, Museum of Fine Arts, Boston: the winged west wind enfolds the Spartan youth he loved — and whose discus death his jealousy would cause.

images.alt: Giovanni Battista Tiepolo, The Triumph of Zephyr and Flora. Ca' Rezzonico, Venice.
images.caption: The Triumph of Zephyr and Flora — Giovanni Battista Tiepolo, c. 1734–35, Ca' Rezzonico, Venice: a ceiling drowned in rose-light where the wind-god's tempest dissolves into garlands, the storm wed to the blossom.

images.alt: François Gérard, Flora Caressed by Zephyr, 1802. Musée de Grenoble.
images.caption: Flora Caressed by Zephyr — François Gérard, 1802, Musée de Grenoble: Neoclassical stillness as the west wind stoops over the goddess of flowers, Ovid's violence refined into a single caress.

images.alt: John William Waterhouse, Flora and the Zephyrs, 1898. Oil on canvas.
images.caption: Flora and the Zephyrs — John William Waterhouse, 1898: the goddess walks in white while the little winds tumble roses across her path — the Zephyr myth softened, at the century's end, to pure perfume.

images.alt: Chiron teaching Achilles the lyre. Roman fresco from Herculaneum, 1st century AD. Museo Archeologico Nazionale, Naples (inv. 9109).
images.caption: The Education of Achilles — the great fresco from Herculaneum's Augusteum, in which the wise centaur guides the boy's hand across the lyre: music before war, the first lesson of the tutor of heroes.

images.alt: Apollo of the Lykeios type, Chiron, and the infant Asclepius. Roman fresco, 1st century AD. Museo Archeologico Nazionale, Naples (inv. 8846).
images.caption: Apollo, Chiron and Asclepius — a Roman wall-painting of the god of Delphi entrusting his son to the centaur's keeping: from Chiron's cave on Pelion, the healing art itself descends.

images.alt: Chiron holding the young Achilles. Etruscan black-figure amphora of the Praxias Group. Cabinet des Médailles, BnF, Paris (De Ridder 913).
images.caption: Chiron holding Achilles — an Etruscan black-figure amphora attributed to the Praxias Group, the fosterage rendered in silhouette: the centaur cradles the child whom Peleus surrendered to his care.

images.alt: Late Roman mosaic from Tipasa showing Thetis retrieving Achilles from Chiron, 4th century AD. Musée national des Antiquités, Algiers.
images.caption: Thetis retrieving Achilles from Chiron — a fourth-century mosaic from Tipasa, set above the discovery on Skyros: the sea-goddess comes to claim her son back from the centaur, and the idyll of Pelion ends.

images.alt: Achilles and Chiron, detail of a white marble sarcophagus, late 3rd century CE. Museo Nazionale Romano, Terme di Diocleziano, Rome.
images.caption: Achilles and Chiron sarcophagus — white marble from the Via Casilina, carved for a Roman tomb in the late third century: even at the edge of death, the patron commissioned the centaur's lesson.

images.alt: Chiron teaching medicine to Asclepius. Southern Italian illuminated medical miscellany, c. 1250. Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Florence (Plut. 73.16).
images.caption: Chiron teaching medicine to Asclepius — a southern Italian medical miscellany of c. 1250 keeps the centaur exactly where the Middle Ages placed him: enthroned at the head of the physician's art.

images.alt: Thetis and Chiron. Engraving by Georg Pencz, 1543.
images.caption: Thetis and Chiron — Georg Pencz's engraving of 1543: the Nereid kneels before the old master of Pelion to plead her son's destiny, the ancient myth recut by a Renaissance burin.
